1	# COR-2268 workspace extraction plan
2	
3	Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2534 (repository change #401). Full plan published in the Workspace extraction implementation plan discussion.
4	
5	Status: implementation plan; no production changes made. Baseline: merged PR #486, commit `0351e4957633761cfec0e57573877f3eabf3aff0`.
6	
7	The next bounded PR should establish `internal/cli/workspace` as the owner of workspace models, manifest operations, and cross-repo graph algorithms. Move the independent tests with those implementations. Keep command assembly and operations that depend on retrieval, privacy, providers, or daemon lifecycle in `cli` until their dependencies have explicit package boundaries.
8	
9	This is the first stage of the workspace split. It removes approximately 1,542 lines of function/type declarations and 33 independent test roots from the CLI compilation unit. It does **not** remove two minutes of test execution. The slower workspace-pattern implementation needs a subsequent extraction.
10	
11	## What the timing evidence establishes
12	
13	The completed local race run passed at this exact source tree. `TestWorkspace*` roots totaled 117.19 seconds of reported elapsed time across 142 tests. That naming group crosses several implementations:
14	
15	| Existing test file | Test roots | Sum of reported elapsed time | Placement in the next PR |
16	| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
17	| `pattern_workspace_semantic_test.go` | 6 | 67.35 s | Retain with the pattern-family implementation |
18	| `workspace_command_regression_test.go` | 15 | 29.96 s | Retain real root-command integration coverage |
19	| `workspace_pattern_failure_regression_test.go` | 4 | 8.16 s | Retain pattern publication/privacy integration coverage |
20	| `workspace_test.go` | 76 | 3.77 s | Split out the 33 independent tests listed below |
21	| `workspace_concurrency_test.go` | 5 | 0.56 s | Retain real lock/setup integration coverage |
22	
23	These are elapsed sums, not additive critical-path savings: some tests use `t.Parallel()`. The 33 initial move candidates each reported `0.00` seconds at the test log's precision. Their value is ownership, a smaller test compilation unit, and independent caching; any build-time benefit must be measured after extraction. Do not claim the earlier 117-second group as this PR's speedup.
24	
25	Evidence: `../workspace-test-weight.json`, `../merged-validation/race.log`, `../workspace-test-dependencies.json`.
26	
27	## Package ownership
28	
29	```text
30	cli assembly and feature adapters
31	  ├── entities
32	  └── workspace
33	        └── internal/base
34	
35	workspace tests ──> internal/clitest
36	```
37	
38	There must be no production or internal-test import from `workspace` back into `cli`. MCP and pattern code may consume workspace models and store operations through their existing CLI assembly. The feature package does not import those consumers.
39	
40	| Destination | Responsibility and current source |
41	| --- | --- |
42	| `internal/cli/workspace/types.go` | `workspaceManifest`, `workspaceRepo`, `workspaceRepoFreshness`, `workspaceAddResult`, `workspaceSummary`; preserve fields and JSON tags |
43	| `internal/cli/workspace/store.go` | Directory resolution, lazy legacy migration, load/write manifest, locked add, membership lock, refresh-result merge; currently distributed through `workspace.go` |
44	| `internal/cli/workspace/validate.go` | Workspace/repo-key/display-name validation, sorting, README rendering, repo-key mismatch predicate, pairing-unsafe scan predicate |
45	| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_types.go` | Contract, symbol reference, cross-edge, aggregate, repo graph index, import reference, and external-symbol reference types |
46	| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_collect.go` | The four SQL collectors at `workspace.go:1217–1446`; callers continue to own validated database acquisition and closure |
47	| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_edges.go` | Cross-repo contract/import/route/GraphQL/channel/resource/symbol matching, ranking, sorting, and bounded edge selection at `workspace.go:1447–2427` |
48	| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_identity.go` | Stable cross-edge IDs, display paths, symbol display, and search score at `workspace.go:2939–3005` |
49	| `internal/cli/workspace/main_test.go` | `TestMain` using `clitest.PinXDGRoots` |
50	| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_edges_test.go`, `validate_test.go` | The existing independent tests, with the same assertions and fixtures |
51	| `internal/cli/workspace_config.go` | Per-invocation construction of workspace store dependencies; analogous to `entities_config.go` |
52	
53	The exact 68 function/type candidates and source locations are recorded in `../workspace-pr2-symbols.json`. Includes neither comments/blank lines nor constants in the 1,542-line estimate. Move the necessary workspace path/schema/display-name constants and the name-validation regexp with their readers. Keep one home for each value; export only values needed by remaining callers.
54	
55	### Code retained in CLI
56	
57	- Cobra command constructors and `runWorkspace*` orchestration remain in `workspace.go` for this PR. They call the new store/algorithm API directly; do not introduce a new package containing only command wrappers.
58	- Keep retrieval results, graph payloads/metrics, regression/review results, and their shared semantic/retrieval model types in CLI. Do not copy those models or move them into `base` merely to satisfy this extraction.
59	- Keep `workspaceSemanticSource`, freshness calculation, member checkout validation, graph-store opening, scan orchestration, and output publication checks in CLI.
60	- Keep `captureWorkspaceRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`, `captureWorkspaceDerivedReadPolicies`, and output revalidation in their existing orchestration paths.
61	- Keep `runSupervisedWatch`, `supervisedWatchLoop`, workspace watch orchestration, signal handling, daemon restart, and shared agent budget logic in CLI.
62	- Keep the generic `writeJSON`, `writeText`, `writeTextToWriter`, and `stickyErrorWriter` helpers in CLI. They happen to live in `workspace.go`, but many unrelated commands use them.
63	- Keep `workspaceFreshnessWarning`, `workspaceRepoBlockNeedsHeader`, and `splitWorkspaceID` in CLI: the first two belong to presentation; the last depends on shared retrieval source prefixes.
64	- Keep `workspace_patterns.go`, `pattern_workspace.go`, and `pattern_workspace_semantic.go` with their implementations and tests until the next boundary proposal.
65	
66	## Shared contracts and dependency injection
67	
68	Use workspace-owned exported models (`Manifest`, `Repo`, `RepoFreshness`, `AddResult`, and graph types). CLI type aliases are acceptable where they preserve existing integration tests and reduce mechanical churn. Do not create copied structs, forwarding functions, copied variables, or const aliases.
69	
70	The store must use the existing filesystem/security implementations through per-instance dependencies. A concrete shape to implement is:
71	
72	```go
73	type StoreDeps struct {
74	    DataDir              func(base.EntireEnv) (string, error)
75	    RejectRootPath       func(string, string) error
76	    RejectPathComponents func(string, string) error
77	    AcquireLock          func(string) (io.Closer, error)
78	    AtomicWrite          func(string, []byte, fs.FileMode) error
79	}
80	
81	type StoreConfig struct {
82	    Env               base.EntireEnv
83	    Deps              StoreDeps
84	    LegacyRepoDirName string
85	    LockDirName       string
86	}
87	```
88	
89	`workspaceStore(env)` in CLI constructs this configuration without resolving paths early. Its `DataDir` adapter invokes `resolvePluginDirs` at the same point the old operation did. Its lock adapter binds the existing `workspace_manifest_locked` error code and `brainWriteLockTimeout`. The path configuration receives the existing repo-store and lock-directory constants. Its atomic writer delegates to the original implementation with the original modes.
90	
91	Expose operations corresponding to the existing behavior: `Dir`, `DirOrEmpty`, `LoadManifest`, `WriteManifest`, `AddRepoLocked`, `AcquireManifestLock`, and `MergeRefreshResult`. Private implementation helpers remain private. Export only graph functions/types actually required by CLI callers; independent tests in package `workspace` can access the remaining private helpers.
92	
93	Important call-site examples:
94	
95	- `setup.go` calls `workspaceStore(env).AddRepoLocked(...)`; the read/modify/write transaction stays inside the store.
96	- MCP loads a workspace model through the store, applies its existing scope filtering, then calls the existing CLI graph/review/regression operation with that filtered manifest.
97	- Pattern code obtains a directory or manifest through the store but retains all existing privacy and publication checks.
98	- `runWorkspaceRemove` continues to hold the **same** manifest lock across load, mutation, write, or whole-workspace deletion. The lock remains outside the directory being deleted.
99	- Graph collectors receive the existing validated `*sql.DB`. Moving collection SQL does not authorize opening arbitrary graph paths in the new package.
100	
101	The Graph impact records show the manifest's consumers in MCP and pattern code and the store's consumers in setup. The generic output helpers have unrelated consumers across the CLI. These are ownership boundaries, not reasons to move those entire feature closures.
102	
103	## Test movement
104	
105	Move only the exact 33 roots in the appendix initially. These tests call the selected algorithms/validators directly and do not require the full CLI root or semantic/provider fixtures. Preserve test names, table cases, assertions, fixture data, and build tags. Allowed edits are package/import changes and symbol qualification needed by the move.
106	
107	Keep the following in CLI, mechanically updating calls to the new API:
108	
109	- `TestWorkspacePropagatesPluginDirErrors`: it verifies the real plugin resolver; replacing it with a fake dependency would weaken the test.
110	- Root command routes, malformed manifests, output failures, path/symlink protections, and legacy migration integration cases.
111	- All five concurrency tests, including `TestConcurrentWorkspaceAddsAllPersist` and `TestConcurrentSetupRegistrationsAllPersist`; they exercise the real lock and setup adapters.
112	- MCP sibling-scope and forged-checkout tests.
113	- Graph-store/cache, privacy, memory/watch, retrieval, regression/review, and pattern integration tests.
114	
115	Do not move integration tests to an external test package that imports `cli` and then count them as independently cached workspace tests. Do not replace real provider/storage fixtures with fakes simply to move a test. More tests can move only when their existing dependencies move intact, with the inventory and measurement updated explicitly.
116	
117	The test movement list is a source/Graph-backed plan, not a compile result. Compile the new package early. If a hidden dependency appears, resolve its actual ownership and update the move list explicitly; never silently omit the test or broaden the extraction into another subsystem.
118	
119	## Implementation sequence
120	
121	1. **Capture the baseline.** Start from current `origin/main` containing #486; record its commit, full runnable test/benchmark/example/fuzz inventory, pinned CLI `main_test.go` hash, and Windows harness settings. The supplied inventory and impact evidence are anchored to `0351e495`; refresh changed anchors if main advances. Do not rename the current branch automatically.
122	2. **Move the graph models and algorithms first.** Add the package and XDG-pinned `TestMain`, move the graph functions and 31 graph tests, qualify production callers, then compile/test CLI and workspace. This validates a boundary with no new filesystem behavior.
123	3. **Move workspace models and the store.** Add the five dependency adapters, move the two remaining validator/predicate tests, update setup/MCP/pattern/CLI callers, and preserve the exact operation order. Maintain a single home for constants and the regexp. No environment-resolution or lock implementation extraction is needed.
124	4. **Run focused integration tests.** Exercise the original scope/privacy, symlink/migration, setup registration, concurrent add/refresh/remove, graph cache, retrieval, and root-command tests against the new adapters. No assertion or expected-output changes should be needed.
125	5. **Verify the extraction mechanically.** Reconcile every runnable name across all packages; compare the moved test bodies after normalizing only package/import/qualified-name changes; confirm no reverse import or duplicate mutable variable; confirm the pinned root `main_test.go` hash is unchanged; run Graph diff for the moves.
126	6. **Run the full gates.** Format, build, vet, full race tests, Windows harness unit tests, and mutation checks. Commit with explicit paths, publish a PR, and require native Windows compile/inventory/shards/non-heavy execution/integrity to pass.
127	7. **Measure the actual benefit.** Capture before/after CLI and workspace compile/test durations with comparable cache conditions. Demonstrate independent workspace test caching using an actual temporary core-only source change, remove it, and verify a clean tree. Report the result without projecting the pattern-family timings onto this PR.
128	
129	## Verification commands and acceptance
130	
131	Use package concurrency one for the local full suite if disk pressure returns. The previous full local race run took 732.7 seconds and passed; maintain enough free space for compilation and fixtures.
132	
133	```sh
134	gofmt -l -s internal/cli
135	go build ./...
136	go vet ./...
137	go test -race ./internal/cli/workspace -count=1
138	go test -race -p=1 ./... -count=1 -timeout=30m
139	python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p 'test_*.py'
140	python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py
141	```
142	
143	Select focused CLI tests from the unchanged inventory, including workspace, concurrent workspace/setup registration, and MCP workspace scope cases. The exact before/after runnable-name set must match, with 33 roots changing packages if the planned list compiles unchanged. Do not rely on equal counts alone, and do not count `TestMain` as a runnable test.
144	
145	No production Windows settings change is planned for this small, independently tested package. Verify that it is included exactly once in the existing non-heavy package path, removed roots no longer appear in CLI inventory, and stale weight entries remain harmless. Run `prepare.py` on native Windows CI; it is not a local macOS dry run. Do not change pinned declarations, shard settings, or weights merely to make validation pass.
146	
147	Acceptance requires all of the following:
148	
149	- New package owns the selected implementation, not wrappers calling back into CLI.
150	- No import cycle, mutable-variable copy, altered serialized shape, new skip, lost runnable root, or weakened assertion.
151	- Original scope, privacy, path safety, membership-lock, stable-ID/order, and output-error tests pass through the new API.
152	- Full local race validation and native Windows CI pass.
153	- PR description reports actual moved roots and measured compile/cache results; it makes no unsupported wall-clock speedup claim.
154	
155	## Following workspace stages
156	
157	The next performance-bearing candidate is the pattern-family implementation in `pattern_workspace.go` and `pattern_workspace_semantic.go`, with `workspace_patterns.go` orchestration considered separately. The six family tests account for the 67.35-second elapsed sum. Before scheduling that extraction, map the complete corpus/schema, SQLite safety, privacy publication, agent-runner, and test-fixture closures. The `twoRepoWorkspace` fixture builds real member corpora through shared pattern builders, so moving those tests is not a file rename.
158	
159	Retain root-command integration tests until their production seams and fixtures allow a move without replacing root coverage. Then reassess retrieval/graph orchestration and watch lifecycle as their own boundaries. Avoid promising a single follow-up PR for all three subsystems before their impacts are measured.
160	
161	CI package selection remains a separate follow-up. Coverage profiles disable ordinary Go result caching in the current workflow; this extraction alone does not implement affected-package selection or eliminate the full coverage run.
162	
163	## Evidence and analysis limits
164	
165	- Recorded constraints: Brain facts `792b23a8f15ba813bf730e72` and `09552bd5a25fd72416a35b5a`, retrieved in `../workspace-plan-recall.json`.
166	- Graph v0.5.0, full profile, committed source: `../workspace-plan-impact-index.json` indexes 145 per-symbol impact reports covering the workspace file's function/type/method surface. `../workspace-pr2-symbols.json` selects the proposed subset.
167	- Boundary edges: `../workspace-boundary-evidence.json`; test dependency evidence: `../workspace-test-dependencies.json`.
168	- Graph reported partial failures in non-Go runner/benchmark JSON, plus incomplete evidence for some data-flow edges. No Go parse failures were reported. Some cross-file names resolve heuristically; source inspection verified the store/MCP boundaries and rejected an apparent production dependency on a test-local variable named `repo`.
169	- The provider does not emit the workspace constants/regexp as symbol definitions in this snapshot. # COR-2268 workspace extraction plan

Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2534 (repository change #401). Full plan published in the Workspace extraction implementation plan discussion.

Status: implementation plan; no production changes made. Baseline: merged PR #486, commit `0351e4957633761cfec0e57573877f3eabf3aff0`.

The next bounded PR should establish `internal/cli/workspace` as the owner of workspace models, manifest operations, and cross-repo graph algorithms. Move the independent tests with those implementations. Keep command assembly and operations that depend on retrieval, privacy, providers, or daemon lifecycle in `cli` until their dependencies have explicit package boundaries.

This is the first stage of the workspace split. It removes approximately 1,542 lines of function/type declarations and 33 independent test roots from the CLI compilation unit. It does **not** remove two minutes of test execution. The slower workspace-pattern implementation needs a subsequent extraction.

## What the timing evidence establishes

The completed local race run passed at this exact source tree. `TestWorkspace*` roots totaled 117.19 seconds of reported elapsed time across 142 tests. That naming group crosses several implementations:

| Existing test file | Test roots | Sum of reported elapsed time | Placement in the next PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `pattern_workspace_semantic_test.go` | 6 | 67.35 s | Retain with the pattern-family implementation |
| `workspace_command_regression_test.go` | 15 | 29.96 s | Retain real root-command integration coverage |
| `workspace_pattern_failure_regression_test.go` | 4 | 8.16 s | Retain pattern publication/privacy integration coverage |
| `workspace_test.go` | 76 | 3.77 s | Split out the 33 independent tests listed below |
| `workspace_concurrency_test.go` | 5 | 0.56 s | Retain real lock/setup integration coverage |

These are elapsed sums, not additive critical-path savings: some tests use `t.Parallel()`. The 33 initial move candidates each reported `0.00` seconds at the test log's precision. Their value is ownership, a smaller test compilation unit, and independent caching; any build-time benefit must be measured after extraction. Do not claim the earlier 117-second group as this PR's speedup.

Evidence: `../workspace-test-weight.json`, `../merged-validation/race.log`, `../workspace-test-dependencies.json`.

## Package ownership

```text
cli assembly and feature adapters
  ├── entities
  └── workspace
        └── internal/base

workspace tests ──> internal/clitest
```

There must be no production or internal-test import from `workspace` back into `cli`. MCP and pattern code may consume workspace models and store operations through their existing CLI assembly. The feature package does not import those consumers.

| Destination | Responsibility and current source |
| --- | --- |
| `internal/cli/workspace/types.go` | `workspaceManifest`, `workspaceRepo`, `workspaceRepoFreshness`, `workspaceAddResult`, `workspaceSummary`; preserve fields and JSON tags |
| `internal/cli/workspace/store.go` | Directory resolution, lazy legacy migration, load/write manifest, locked add, membership lock, refresh-result merge; currently distributed through `workspace.go` |
| `internal/cli/workspace/validate.go` | Workspace/repo-key/display-name validation, sorting, README rendering, repo-key mismatch predicate, pairing-unsafe scan predicate |
| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_types.go` | Contract, symbol reference, cross-edge, aggregate, repo graph index, import reference, and external-symbol reference types |
| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_collect.go` | The four SQL collectors at `workspace.go:1217–1446`; callers continue to own validated database acquisition and closure |
| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_edges.go` | Cross-repo contract/import/route/GraphQL/channel/resource/symbol matching, ranking, sorting, and bounded edge selection at `workspace.go:1447–2427` |
| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_identity.go` | Stable cross-edge IDs, display paths, symbol display, and search score at `workspace.go:2939–3005` |
| `internal/cli/workspace/main_test.go` | `TestMain` using `clitest.PinXDGRoots` |
| `internal/cli/workspace/graph_edges_test.go`, `validate_test.go` | The existing independent tests, with the same assertions and fixtures |
| `internal/cli/workspace_config.go` | Per-invocation construction of workspace store dependencies; analogous to `entities_config.go` |

The exact 68 function/type candidates and source locations are recorded in `../workspace-pr2-symbols.json`. Includes neither comments/blank lines nor constants in the 1,542-line estimate. Move the necessary workspace path/schema/display-name constants and the name-validation regexp with their readers. Keep one home for each value; export only values needed by remaining callers.

### Code retained in CLI

- Cobra command constructors and `runWorkspace*` orchestration remain in `workspace.go` for this PR. They call the new store/algorithm API directly; do not introduce a new package containing only command wrappers.
- Keep retrieval results, graph payloads/metrics, regression/review results, and their shared semantic/retrieval model types in CLI. Do not copy those models or move them into `base` merely to satisfy this extraction.
- Keep `workspaceSemanticSource`, freshness calculation, member checkout validation, graph-store opening, scan orchestration, and output publication checks in CLI.
- Keep `captureWorkspaceRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`, `captureWorkspaceDerivedReadPolicies`, and output revalidation in their existing orchestration paths.
- Keep `runSupervisedWatch`, `supervisedWatchLoop`, workspace watch orchestration, signal handling, daemon restart, and shared agent budget logic in CLI.
- Keep the generic `writeJSON`, `writeText`, `writeTextToWriter`, and `stickyErrorWriter` helpers in CLI. They happen to live in `workspace.go`, but many unrelated commands use them.
- Keep `workspaceFreshnessWarning`, `workspaceRepoBlockNeedsHeader`, and `splitWorkspaceID` in CLI: the first two belong to presentation; the last depends on shared retrieval source prefixes.
- Keep `workspace_patterns.go`, `pattern_workspace.go`, and `pattern_workspace_semantic.go` with their implementations and tests until the next boundary proposal.

## Shared contracts and dependency injection

Use workspace-owned exported models (`Manifest`, `Repo`, `RepoFreshness`, `AddResult`, and graph types). CLI type aliases are acceptable where they preserve existing integration tests and reduce mechanical churn. Do not create copied structs, forwarding functions, copied variables, or const aliases.

The store must use the existing filesystem/security implementations through per-instance dependencies. A concrete shape to implement is:

```go
type StoreDeps struct {
    DataDir              func(base.EntireEnv) (string, error)
    RejectRootPath       func(string, string) error
    RejectPathComponents func(string, string) error
    AcquireLock          func(string) (io.Closer, error)
    AtomicWrite          func(string, []byte, fs.FileMode) error
}

type StoreConfig struct {
    Env               base.EntireEnv
    Deps              StoreDeps
    LegacyRepoDirName string
    LockDirName       string
}
```

`workspaceStore(env)` in CLI constructs this configuration without resolving paths early. Its `DataDir` adapter invokes `resolvePluginDirs` at the same point the old operation did. Its lock adapter binds the existing `workspace_manifest_locked` error code and `brainWriteLockTimeout`. The path configuration receives the existing repo-store and lock-directory constants. Its atomic writer delegates to the original implementation with the original modes.

Expose operations corresponding to the existing behavior: `Dir`, `DirOrEmpty`, `LoadManifest`, `WriteManifest`, `AddRepoLocked`, `AcquireManifestLock`, and `MergeRefreshResult`. Private implementation helpers remain private. Export only graph functions/types actually required by CLI callers; independent tests in package `workspace` can access the remaining private helpers.

Important call-site examples:

- `setup.go` calls `workspaceStore(env).AddRepoLocked(...)`; the read/modify/write transaction stays inside the store.
- MCP loads a workspace model through the store, applies its existing scope filtering, then calls the existing CLI graph/review/regression operation with that filtered manifest.
- Pattern code obtains a directory or manifest through the store but retains all existing privacy and publication checks.
- `runWorkspaceRemove` continues to hold the **same** manifest lock across load, mutation, write, or whole-workspace deletion. The lock remains outside the directory being deleted.
- Graph collectors receive the existing validated `*sql.DB`. Moving collection SQL does not authorize opening arbitrary graph paths in the new package.

The Graph impact records show the manifest's consumers in MCP and pattern code and the store's consumers in setup. The generic output helpers have unrelated consumers across the CLI. These are ownership boundaries, not reasons to move those entire feature closures.

## Test movement

Move only the exact 33 roots in the appendix initially. These tests call the selected algorithms/validators directly and do not require the full CLI root or semantic/provider fixtures. Preserve test names, table cases, assertions, fixture data, and build tags. Allowed edits are package/import changes and symbol qualification needed by the move.

Keep the following in CLI, mechanically updating calls to the new API:

- `TestWorkspacePropagatesPluginDirErrors`: it verifies the real plugin resolver; replacing it with a fake dependency would weaken the test.
- Root command routes, malformed manifests, output failures, path/symlink protections, and legacy migration integration cases.
- All five concurrency tests, including `TestConcurrentWorkspaceAddsAllPersist` and `TestConcurrentSetupRegistrationsAllPersist`; they exercise the real lock and setup adapters.
- MCP sibling-scope and forged-checkout tests.
- Graph-store/cache, privacy, memory/watch, retrieval, regression/review, and pattern integration tests.

Do not move integration tests to an external test package that imports `cli` and then count them as independently cached workspace tests. Do not replace real provider/storage fixtures with fakes simply to move a test. More tests can move only when their existing dependencies move intact, with the inventory and measurement updated explicitly.

The test movement list is a source/Graph-backed plan, not a compile result. Compile the new package early. If a hidden dependency appears, resolve its actual ownership and update the move list explicitly; never silently omit the test or broaden the extraction into another subsystem.

## Implementation sequence

1. **Capture the baseline.** Start from current `origin/main` containing #486; record its commit, full runnable test/benchmark/example/fuzz inventory, pinned CLI `main_test.go` hash, and Windows harness settings. The supplied inventory and impact evidence are anchored to `0351e495`; refresh changed anchors if main advances. Do not rename the current branch automatically.
2. **Move the graph models and algorithms first.** Add the package and XDG-pinned `TestMain`, move the graph functions and 31 graph tests, qualify production callers, then compile/test CLI and workspace. This validates a boundary with no new filesystem behavior.
3. **Move workspace models and the store.** Add the five dependency adapters, move the two remaining validator/predicate tests, update setup/MCP/pattern/CLI callers, and preserve the exact operation order. Maintain a single home for constants and the regexp. No environment-resolution or lock implementation extraction is needed.
4. **Run focused integration tests.** Exercise the original scope/privacy, symlink/migration, setup registration, concurrent add/refresh/remove, graph cache, retrieval, and root-command tests against the new adapters. No assertion or expected-output changes should be needed.
5. **Verify the extraction mechanically.** Reconcile every runnable name across all packages; compare the moved test bodies after normalizing only package/import/qualified-name changes; confirm no reverse import or duplicate mutable variable; confirm the pinned root `main_test.go` hash is unchanged; run Graph diff for the moves.
6. **Run the full gates.** Format, build, vet, full race tests, Windows harness unit tests, and mutation checks. Commit with explicit paths, publish a PR, and require native Windows compile/inventory/shards/non-heavy execution/integrity to pass.
7. **Measure the actual benefit.** Capture before/after CLI and workspace compile/test durations with comparable cache conditions. Demonstrate independent workspace test caching using an actual temporary core-only source change, remove it, and verify a clean tree. Report the result without projecting the pattern-family timings onto this PR.

## Verification commands and acceptance

Use package concurrency one for the local full suite if disk pressure returns. The previous full local race run took 732.7 seconds and passed; maintain enough free space for compilation and fixtures.

```sh
gofmt -l -s internal/cli
go build ./...
go vet ./...
go test -race ./internal/cli/workspace -count=1
go test -race -p=1 ./... -count=1 -timeout=30m
python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p 'test_*.py'
python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py
```

Select focused CLI tests from the unchanged inventory, including workspace, concurrent workspace/setup registration, and MCP workspace scope cases. The exact before/after runnable-name set must match, with 33 roots changing packages if the planned list compiles unchanged. Do not rely on equal counts alone, and do not count `TestMain` as a runnable test.

No production Windows settings change is planned for this small, independently tested package. Verify that it is included exactly once in the existing non-heavy package path, removed roots no longer appear in CLI inventory, and stale weight entries remain harmless. Run `prepare.py` on native Windows CI; it is not a local macOS dry run. Do not change pinned declarations, shard settings, or weights merely to make validation pass.

Acceptance requires all of the following:

- New package owns the selected implementation, not wrappers calling back into CLI.
- No import cycle, mutable-variable copy, altered serialized shape, new skip, lost runnable root, or weakened assertion.
- Original scope, privacy, path safety, membership-lock, stable-ID/order, and output-error tests pass through the new API.
- Full local race validation and native Windows CI pass.
- PR description reports actual moved roots and measured compile/cache results; it makes no unsupported wall-clock speedup claim.

## Following workspace stages

The next performance-bearing candidate is the pattern-family implementation in `pattern_workspace.go` and `pattern_workspace_semantic.go`, with `workspace_patterns.go` orchestration considered separately. The six family tests account for the 67.35-second elapsed sum. Before scheduling that extraction, map the complete corpus/schema, SQLite safety, privacy publication, agent-runner, and test-fixture closures. The `twoRepoWorkspace` fixture builds real member corpora through shared pattern builders, so moving those tests is not a file rename.

Retain root-command integration tests until their production seams and fixtures allow a move without replacing root coverage. Then reassess retrieval/graph orchestration and watch lifecycle as their own boundaries. Avoid promising a single follow-up PR for all three subsystems before their impacts are measured.

CI package selection remains a separate follow-up. Coverage profiles disable ordinary Go result caching in the current workflow; this extraction alone does not implement affected-package selection or eliminate the full coverage run.

## Evidence and analysis limits

- Recorded constraints: Brain facts `792b23a8f15ba813bf730e72` and `09552bd5a25fd72416a35b5a`, retrieved in `../workspace-plan-recall.json`.
- Graph v0.5.0, full profile, committed source: `../workspace-plan-impact-index.json` indexes 145 per-symbol impact reports covering the workspace file's function/type/method surface. `../workspace-pr2-symbols.json` selects the proposed subset.
- Boundary edges: `../workspace-boundary-evidence.json`; test dependency evidence: `../workspace-test-dependencies.json`.
- Graph reported partial failures in non-Go runner/benchmark JSON, plus incomplete evidence for some data-flow edges. No Go parse failures were reported. Some cross-file names resolve heuristically; source inspection verified the store/MCP boundaries and rejected an apparent production dependency on a test-local variable named `repo`.
- The provider does not emit the workspace constants/regexp as symbol definitions in this snapshot. Impact lookups returned related-symbol suggestions rather than exact constant/regexp definitions. Their current literal/name uses were checked directly and recorded in `../workspace-plan-constant-uses.json`; recheck changed uses during implementation. # COR-2268 PR 1: foundation packages + entities extraction

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** First extraction PR for COR-2268 — create the shared foundation packages and move the `entities` command cluster out of `internal/cli`, proving the whole split pipeline with CI green.

**Architecture:** Three-layer DAG: `internal/cli` (root assembly + not-yet-extracted clusters) → `internal/cli/entities` (pilot feature package) → `internal/cli/internal/base` (shared prod helpers, incl. hook-seam vars). `internal/cli/internal/clitest` holds cross-package test support (XDG pin, shared fakes); test files only. Feature packages never import `internal/cli`; `internal/cli` imports feature packages.

**Tech Stack:** Go 1.27.2, cobra, stdlib only. No new dependencies.

**Spec:** Linear COR-2268 (https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2268). Dependency measurements: `.context/graph-symbols.ndjson`, `.context/graph-edges.ndjson` analysis summarized below.

## Continuation notes (2026-10-24)

Task 1 was already committed as 94ef9dad. Current implementation follows the three-layer DAG, with source-verified adjustments:

- `main_test.go` calls `resolvePluginDirs` and the XDG constants directly. Moving all of env.go conflicts with both the frozen file and the no-forwarding-shims requirement. Move shared environment/storage types and retain environment resolution in cli.
- The concrete runner depends on Git hardening; manifest loading depends on source manifests, checkpoint formats, and migration logic. Keep those implementations in cli and inject per-invocation operations through `entities.Config` / `entities.Deps`.
- Move safe reads and their single-home bounds, path resolution, JSON/string helpers, checkpoint trailer parsing, GitScalar, fact locus helpers, and shared options/types into base.
- Extract entities commands, history/cache reads, refresh, and provenance. Retain storage/privacy/session adapters in cli. Keep integration tests that require private CLI fixtures in cli, as Task 3 permits. Move the independent provenance tie-break test and safe-read unit tests unchanged apart from names/imports.
- Exact runnable-name inventory: 3,459 before and after (includes benchmarks/examples/fuzz roots); no missing or added names. Pinned TestMain is byte-identical.
- `go build ./...`, focused tests, `go vet ./...`, race tests for entities/base/clitest, and all 41 Windows harness unit tests pass.
- Full non-race repository suite passes with package concurrency 1; all four mutation cases pass. The local full race run hit ENOSPC, but full macOS/Ubuntu race and coverage CI jobs pass. Native Windows compile/plan, race vet, all six shards, non-heavy packages, and final coverage/integrity verification pass.
- `prepare.py` is not a portable dry run: it requires a clean tracked checkout and GOOS=windows/GOARCH=amd64/CGO_ENABLED=1. Native Windows CI verified the actual inventory and partition.
- Fetched origin/main: PR #485 independently changed the harness to six shards and updated weights. This extraction does not modify the harness.

- Rebased on origin/main and pushed commits `b1781911` (clitest) and `2f648d6a` (extraction). PR: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/486. Repository CI is green. The isolated-cache demonstration passes: an actual core-only source addition reruns CLI tests while entities/base/clitest remain cached. Evidence: `.context/cache-demo.log`. Temporary probe and cache were removed. External Entire Gates/Partial Gates remain pending at preparation time.

## Global Constraints

- Tests are moved, not rewritten: same assertions, same fixtures (ticket acceptance).
- Do NOT modify `internal/cli/main_test.go` — its normalized source SHA-256 is pinned in `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json` (`expectedTestMainDeclarations`); any edit fails the Windows prepare job closed. PR 1 makes zero changes under `tools/ci-bench/`.
- Hook-seam vars (`defaultMaxReadBytes`, `maxManifestBytes`, …) get exactly ONE home. When one moves to `base`, every reader and every test that swaps it references `base.<Name>`. Never leave a `var old = base.New` shim for a VAR — swapping the shim would not affect base readers (split-brain). Function and const shims are forbidden too: sed-rename call sites instead.
- Type moves use aliases in `internal/cli` (`type Options = base.Options`) so `cmd/entire-brain/main.go` (the only external importer) and the ~200 unmoved files compile unchanged.
- Every new test package has a `main_test.go` whose `TestMain` calls `clitest.PinXDGRoots` — without it, tests write junk into the developer's real brain store (documented escape: 1,193 fallthroughs).
- Format gate before push: `gofmt -l -s` empty + `go vet ./...` (repo has no oxfmt binary; CI gates on these).
- Commits: explicit file names in `git add`, never `-A`/`.`. End messages with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.

## Review Focus

1. Moved tests silently vanishing (a `go test` typo or build-tag slip drops them with no failure) → Task 3 step compares `go test -list '.*'` counts before/after across the two packages.
2. New package escaping the XDG pin and writing `~/.local/share/entire/...` → Task 1 test asserts the pin; Task 3 requires `entities/main_test.go` before any test file moves.
3. Hook-var split-brain (test swaps a cli-local copy while base readers use another) → Task 2 step greps that no moved var name still exists in `internal/cli/*.go`.
4. Windows plain-`go test` file-lock flake on the new package (the reason cli runs precompiled in nightly; cannot reproduce locally) → called out in PR body as the thing to watch on the first Windows CI run; entities spawns no detached workers, so expected clean.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove a guide.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

The six tests still rely on real workspace privacy gates, manifests, and transcript storage, so I need to keep their fixtures untouched until those dependencies get properly separated rather than substituting permissive stubs. This is a substantial task, so I'll follow the standard methodology: graph preflight, recall prior decisions on privacy gates, map the dependency closure of those six tests, then plan, implement, test, and open a PR.

Main merge validated. Next I'll separate the six heavy workspace-family integration tests from their real privacy gate, manifest, and transcript storage dependencies, starting with a Graph preflight and targeted recall.

Most callers of loadSessionReadGuard pass a non-nil manifest, and since exportManifest is a CLI type, moving this function wholesale would require either relocating the large export.go or rewriting roughly 35 call sites. This privacy-core extraction is clearly turning into its own multi-step project.

I'm sketching three slices by increasing coupling: a bounded tombstone state layer (types, loaders, path normalization, constants) with dependencies to check like MaxManifestBytes and the brain-relative atomic writer; a privacy transaction layer depending on brainstore reads/writes and session prefixes; and finally the guard core with policy capture, which is the biggest since it touches exportManifest across all those call sites. Given the established bounded-PR cadence, I'm weighing how to sequence these.

Following that pattern, the next PR would bundle slices 1+2 into brainstore with their own tests, unblocking the guard move and patterns-side gates—though that standalone value feels modest. So I'm considering an alternative: moving the pattern_workspace implementation files into patterns with injected Config/Deps for privacy functions, leaving tests in CLI for now, since that pulls a large chunk of impl code out of the CLI compile unit and establishes the workspace-pattern API sooner.

But I'm realizing #494 already moved family proposal/validation/caching into patterns, so the semantic workspace file is now mostly thin orchestration over the core proposal logic—meaning what's left on the CLI side is really just orchestration plus corpus build. Given the recorded fact that the six integration tests depend on real privacy gates and storage until separated, and the session's own note that the patterns/privacy migration is next, I'll commit to the tombstones + privacy transactions slice into brainstore and start verifying its dependency details.

I need to trace a few things: how the versioned JSON body decoding closure works, how the brain file writer atomically persists data and whether brainstore has an equivalent, how many places reference the session ID prefix and the unsupported-version error, where the history directory constant is used, and which tests exercise these layers independently. I also want to check the callers of session tombstone saving across exclude/include/purge and the CLI—since saving stays used by the CLI, I should move the function together with its type into one home.

Since almost all guard callers use a real manifest, moving the guard would require a signature redesign across ~35 sites — too large to bundle with the state layer in this PR. I'll scope the next slice to migrating the tombstone state and privacy-transaction layer into `brainstore`, leaving guard/policy for later, and now I'll verify the remaining dependencies.

	privacyStateError      = "error"

You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow.
